title: Retain C implementation for parser
decided: The team decided to keep the existing C implementation for parser/core.c. To address memory safety concerns and buffer overflow risks, the team will instead integrate AddressSanitizer and LibFuzzer into the CI pipeline.

rejected.why: The Rust prototype resulted in a 2x performance regression (145 MB/s vs 295 MB/s) due to mandatory slice bounds checks and UTF-8 verification. Additionally, there were concerns regarding the introduction of cargo/rustc as mandatory build dependencies and the potential loss of C99 portability for embedded toolchains.

sources.quote: I propose that we rewrite parser/core.c in Rust. Our recent security audit flagged several memory safety concerns and buffer overflow risks in the C parser.
sources.exact_quote: I propose that we rewrite parser/core.c in Rust. Our recent security audit flagged several memory safety concerns and buffer overflow risks in the C parser.

sources.quote: introducing Rust adds cargo and rustc as mandatory build dependencies. Our project has always targeted strict C99 portability across embedded toolchains.
sources.exact_quote: introducing Rust adds cargo and rustc as mandatory build dependencies. Our project has always targeted strict C99 portability across embedded toolchains.

sources.quote: The routines in parser/core.c are called millions of times per second in hot loops by our C engine. Any foreign function interface crossing could degrade parsing throughput.
sources.exact_quote: The routines in parser/core.c are called millions of times per second in hot loops by our C engine. Any foreign function interface crossing could degrade parsing throughput.

sources.quote: The Rust prototype in parser/core.c is 2x slower in benchmarks compared to the C implementation (145 MB/s vs 295 MB/s). The regression comes from mandatory slice bounds checks and UTF-8 verification.
